transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

Lately I just don’t care about the art shows, the mentoring, or even my photography anymore; nothing feels worth doing. My wife was really the one who pushed me to come in because I've just completely shut down.
Have you ever had periods in your life where you felt the exact opposite—unusually energetic, hyperactive, or on top of the world, perhaps needing very little sleep?

Yes, right after I retired, I went through a phase where I felt almost high on life, buzzing with energy and taking on an overwhelming number of art shows, mentoring, and writing projects. I felt uniquely capable of handling it all, and I'd get incredibly snappish with my wife if she even suggested I slow down.
How long did that period of high energy and feeling 'high on life' last? Also, did you find you needed much less sleep than usual during that time?

That high-energy period lasted for several weeks, maybe a couple of months, shortly after I retired. As for my sleep during that time, I honestly can't clearly remember how much I was getting because everything was moving so fast.
During that high-energy period, did you notice your thoughts racing, or did others tell you that you were talking much faster than usual?

Yes, absolutely. My thoughts were racing so fast it felt like a dozen radios were blaring in my head at once and I couldn't slow them down. My wife even joked she couldn't get a word in edgewise because I'd launch into rapid, unstoppable monologues about my projects without pausing.

During that high-energy period, did your behavior cause any serious problems in your life, or did it ever lead to a hospital stay? Also, did you experience anything unusual like hearing or seeing things that others couldn't?

It definitely caused problems—I got furious with my wife whenever she told me to slow down, and I overcommitted so much that I ended up missing my own art exhibition and backing out of my mentoring. I was never hospitalized for it, though, and I certainly didn't see or hear anything unusual.
Are you still able to manage basic daily activities like eating, bathing, and getting out of bed, or has this low mood made it nearly impossible to do even those things?

I technically get out of bed, but everything feels incredibly difficult and slow, like I'm wading through mud. I mostly shuffle around the house or stare blankly at the kettle, and my wife has had to take over almost all household responsibilities. I just sit in my chair and can't bring myself to manage even simple daily routines.

During this current period of feeling so low, have you experienced any unusual thoughts, like feeling excessively guilty about things that aren't your fault, or hearing or seeing things that others can't?

I feel like a useless old fraud who has let everyone down by dropping the ball on my mentoring and the art exhibition. I constantly replay past missteps from my career and marriage as if they're unforgivable sins, but I definitely haven't seen or heard things that aren't there.

Do you feel so strongly about these mistakes that you believe you are completely ruined financially, or do you feel that your body is physically failing or rotting inside, even if there is no medical proof of it?

No, nothing like that—I don't believe we are ruined financially, and I don't feel like my body is physically rotting. It's more of a deep, heavy guilt and feeling like an absolute failure who has let everyone down.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a current severe depressive episode characterized by a loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities (photography, mentoring, art), profound psychomotor retardation ('wading through mud', shuffling, staring blankly), and excessive guilt/feelings of worthlessness ('useless old fraud', viewing past missteps as 'unforgivable sins'). The severity is marked by his inability to manage basic daily routines, requiring his wife to take over household responsibilities. Psychotic symptoms (such as delusions of ruin, somatic delusions, or hallucinations) were explicitly denied. Additionally, the patient has a clear history of a manic/hypomanic episode shortly after retirement, characterized by elevated and irritable mood, racing thoughts, pressured speech, grandiosity, and hyper-activity lasting several weeks. This clinical picture satisfies the criteria for Bipolar Affective Disorder, Current Episode Severe Depression Without Psychotic Symptoms (F31.4).
